newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dlr flummoxed by opaque rate policy.
newsitem.headline: Australian dlr flummoxed by opaque rate policy.

text.p: The Australian dollar finished a shade softer Friday but well above recent lows, reflecting relief another week had passed with no cut in official rates and frustration that it may yet happen in the month ahead.

The Reserve Bank's silence after its monthly board meeting Tuesday left many convinced it was merely on hold until key inflation and wages data on July 23/24 and if these were as benign as the expected, ease soon afterwards.
Only a brave few thought the year-old easing cycle had actually ended, which was why the so many players were happy to have bids at U$0.7470 and offers at US$0.7550 at the same time.
By 5.30 pm (0730 GMT) the dollar was striving to find traction at US$0.7519/24 after slipping to an early US$0.7515/20 from US$0.7530/35 late Thursday.

The going was made harder by persistent rumours an Asian bank was protecting a big strangle option atop US$0.7570, although traders said this sort of talk often reflected the range bound mentality of the market more than reality.

The dollar had reached as high as US$0.7548 overnight but faltered when the gold price slid on news the Reserve Bank of Australia said it had sold 167 tonnes, or two thirds of its total gold reserves, over the past six months.

There was a time in the 1980s when the A$ matched every twitch in the gold price, largely as the yellow metal was then bought as a hedge against inflation. If gold was rising it usually meant commodity prices in general were heading higher and was thus a useful barometer for the commodity-sensitive A$.

But the relationship broke down this decade as inflation shrank around the world and gold lost its relevance as a hedging tool -- studies have shown the A$ had a far higher correlation with aluminium and copper than it ever had with gold.
But the weakness in precious metals did threaten to Have an indirect impact via the Commodity Research Bureau index.

The index is far from a perfect match to Australian exports -- it includes such un-Australian products as cocoa, coffee and hog futures and excludes the country's largest export earner; coal. But it is influential with U.S. investors who regard it as a crucial guide to general trends in world commodity prices.
Gold is a part of this, although only one of 17 commodities covered, and contributed to a 1.85 point drop in the index to 235.57 on Thursday.
The fall was significant since it breached major support around 236.00 and left the index at its lowest level since August 1995.
Chart watchers said the breach was bearish and threatened to return the index to 233.00 if not the 1995 low of 229.31.

Dollar bulls had been rather hoping stronger commodity prices would compensate for the currency's dwindling yield attraction in the second half of this year, particularly as it seemed likely the RBA would yet cut official rates this cycle.
Many suspected that such an easing, without the promise of commodity support, would see the dollar plumb 73 cents.
The next signpost on the policy trail will be employment figures for June next Thursday which should confirm the labour market was flat at best.

A benign reading on inflation and wages later in the month, as analysts expect, would set the scene for another 0.5 point cut in cash rates to 5.0 percent. On the crosses the dollar was off at 85.15/25 yen from 86.10/20 late Thursday and at 57.3 in trade weighted terms from a previous 57.6 close.

It found support from a modest U.S. jobs report which showed the unemployment rate edging up to 5.0 percent in June from 4.8 percent. The data was taken as lessening the chance of the Federal Reserve hiking rates at its next meeting in August. Such a move would have taken U.S. rates above those here and dealt a psychological blow to the A$. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
